The Bering Sea. A shallow marginal sea of the North Pacific separating Alaska from eastern Russia by roughly fifty-five miles at its narrowest point, the Bering Strait. Extraordinarily rich in marine life and mineral resources, it has been contested territory between indigenous peoples, Russians, and Americans. The sea is a critical fishery, particularly for salmon and crab, and has become a strategic point in climate change and geopolitical competition for Arctic resources.

The Bering Sea is named for Danish explorer Vitus Bering, who explored it in the 1730s under Russian sponsorship. The strait at its northern end is also named for him. The Bering Strait, fifty-six miles wide, is the only water barrier between Asia and North America. During ice ages when sea levels dropped, land bridges called Beringia connected the continents, allowing human migration.

The Bering Sea is one of the world's most productive fisheries. Salmon, crab, pollock, and halibut support major commercial and subsistence fisheries, particularly for Alaska. Indigenous peoples including the Yupik, Inupiat, Chukchi, and Siberian Yup'ik have inhabited its coasts for thousands of years and maintain traditional subsistence practices. The Yukon River flows into it, providing freshwater input and connecting interior North America to the sea.

Climate change is rapidly warming the Bering Sea, shifting fish stocks and threatening Arctic marine mammals. This warming is also opening new shipping routes and resource exploration opportunities. The region has geopolitical significance due to Russian-American boundary disputes, subsistence rights for indigenous peoples, and emerging Arctic competition for natural gas and minerals, making it strategically important.
